As Yashraj Sharma observed in an article in Al Jazeera, it was a “cold and formal depiction far removed from his description of the US president as a ‘good friend’ in previous years.” The Trump-Modi phone call came at a time when already fraying bilateral relations hit yet another difficult phase. Ten days earlier, Trump signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act (SRIA) of 2026, which gives the U.S. president the authority to impose up to 100 percent tariffs on countries that continue to purchase Russian oil and gas. India, which is among the largest buyers of Russian energy, could potentially be impacted. India-U.S. cooperation has deepened and widened over the past two decades. Despite “complexities,” ties were expected to grow under Trump; the outlook was upbeat. However, Trump 2.0 has not been good for the partnership. Within weeks of the inauguration of Trump’s second presidential term, ties began unravelling not only over tariffs and immigration but also Washington’s cozying up to Pakistan on a raft of issues, including terrorism, an issue that Delhi is highly sensitive about. India was among the countries that were hit the hardest by Trump’s “reciprocal tariffs” announced last year. Adding insult to injury, India was then slapped with another 25 percent “punitive tariffs” for buying Russian oil. Should the U.S.

articles.title: Concerns About ‘WWII Allies’ at US-China Summit
articles.excerpt: At the U.S.-China summit in September 2026, both leaders spoke of the fact that the United States and China had been allies in World War II and had fought together. Of course, the United States and China (the Republic of China) were indeed Allied nations in WWII and fought together against Japan and others, and if the summit remarks were intended simply to reaffirm that historical fact and invoke shared memory, then they should give rise to no particular concern. It is also worth recalling that in 2015, the 70th anniversary of the end of the war, U.S.-China relations were relatively stable, and China was emphasizing that it had fought alongside the United States and other major Western powers as key members of the Allied coalition, and had jointly created the postwar order. At that time, China was using the phrase “New Model of Major-Country Relations” in its relations with the United States. If the invocation of wartime partnership at the recent summit was intended to evoke memories of that 2015 period and signal an intention to restore the “New Model of Major-Country Relations,” that too would be comprehensible as a matter of Chinese policy. However, more than ten years have now passed since 2015, and China’s narrative on history today is different from what it once was. So the fact that wartime partnership was raised by both sides at this summit is, in fact, a cause for concern. To explain, it is necessary to look at how China has recently been employing its historical narrative — with particular attention to its relationship with Russia. The COVID-19 pandemic of 2020 and China’s response to it, together with Russia’s war in Ukraine beginning in 2022, generated widespread international criticism of both countries. That criticism brought China and Russia closer together, and the two countries more openly positioned themselves in opposition to Western nations.

articles.title: Philippines Rejects Chinese Claim to ‘Sovereign Rights’ Over Waters Around Batanes
articles.excerpt: The Philippine government today rejected China’s assertion that it has sovereign rights and jurisdiction over waters off Batanes, the country’s northernmost province, a day after the Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) drove away a Chinese research vessel operating in the area. The PCG said yesterday that it had deployed its largest vessel and an aircraft to challenge the Jia Ha Ke 7, a Chinese research ship, that had been “loitering” around 37 nautical miles northwest of Batanes for the past four days. During the confrontation, PCG spokesperson Jay Tarriela said that a China Coast Guard vessel also moved in and “repeatedly tried to shield the research vessel and block the PCG ship.” The Philippine operation nonetheless “successfully disrupted the unauthorized marine scientific research” being conducted by the Jia He Ke 7 and “compelled it to leave the position it had held off Itbayat, Batanes, for four days.” China’s embassy in Manila responded by claiming that the Chinese research vessel was “conducting normal operations in waters under China’s jurisdiction in accordance with international law.” It urged the Philippines to “genuinely respect China’s sovereign rights and jurisdiction in the relevant waters,” and to cease its “provocative interference with China’s normal scientific research activities.” In a statement today, the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) said it “firmly and strongly rejects” the Chinese claims of sovereignty over the waters around Batanes, a group of islands lying midway between Taiwan and the Philippines’ Luzon island. It argued that the Chinese research vessel was operating well within the country’s 200-nautical-mile Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ), where, according to the U.N.

articles.title: Indonesia Needs to Do More to Tackle the Region’s Transboundary Haze Problem
articles.excerpt: Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto is the key leader in ASEAN who can and should do better in haze management in the coming years. The current haze situation affecting Southeast Asia is, to a certain extent, a reflection of his leadership and management, given that most of it stems from fires happening in his country. Forests and peatlands in Indonesia have been burning substantially this year and millions of people in Southeast Asia are suffering as a result. In early September, Kuching had the worst air quality of any large city on earth. Malaysian authorities declared a state of emergency in the Serian district of Sarawak, as the Air Pollutant Index exceeded 500. The Philippines closed schools throughout Metro Manila and more than 12 provinces. The regional haze monitor in ASEAN reached level three, the most severe on the scale. Indonesia needs to improve its leadership on the haze management issue. Fire has been used to clear land as it is cheaper than alternative methods. Plantations, companies, and farmers burn the vegetation before the planting season, instead of paying for mechanical clearing. The drained peatlands of Sumatra and Kalimantan also get burnt and this adds fuel to the fire. These fires continue for weeks and release even more toxic particles than an ordinary forest fire. Due to the current El Niño climate cycle, there are drier and longer dry seasons, worsening the situation, as experienced in 1997, 2015, and 2019. The solutions are relatively straightforward. They are to rewet the drained peatland, enforce a moratorium on new plantation permits in forest and peat areas, punish the recalcitrant companies, and publicize their names so they can be held responsible. Importantly, there needs to be close tracking of fires and smallholder burning, as well as enhanced local fire-response capacity so as to minimize, control, and extinguish fires before they get out of control. Satellite technology can be used to facilitate the tracking too.

articles.title: A Tajik Bank Shuts Side Door for Russian Cardholders
articles.excerpt: Tajikistan’s Humo Bank has warned its Russian clients that their cards will be blocked on October 1 unless they visit one of its offices in Tajikistan by September 30 to undergo biometric identification. “If you can’t come to Tajikistan in person and complete the identification, unfortunately, your card will be closed,” the bank told Russian news site Lenta.ru, advising clients to move their remaining balances to ruble cards before the deadline. The bank cited the need to protect clients from fraud. A Russian client, however, told the Telegram channel Ostorozhno Novosti that the bank’s support staff explained it had decided to restrict services for “certain categories of non-resident individuals” whose cards were opened online. She said a transfer of about 300 euros had been stuck for a week and that the bank had stopped responding to her complaints. Humo offered her a new card if she traveled to Tajikistan, valid only for the duration of her legal stay and for no longer than a year. With Visa and Mastercard gone from Russia since 2022, Russians have relied on cards issued in “friendly” countries to make payments abroad. When Kazakhstan limited non-resident cards to 12 months and required in-person issuance in January 2025, intermediaries moved their business to Tajikistan, Kyrgyzstan, and Uzbekistan. Humo and the International Bank of Tajikistan began offering remotely issued five-year cards in U.S. dollars and euros, sold through intermediaries for roughly 15,000 to 70,000 rubles. Humo is a newcomer to banking. Owned by the Japanese investment holding Gojo & Company, the former microcredit deposit organization received a full banking license from the National Bank of Tajikistan in July 2025. It was also among the few Tajik financial institutions with access to Visa Direct, a real-time payment service that became a conduit for Russian money headed to Europe.

articles.title: Trouble in Shangri-La? Why Bruneians Are Going to Australia for Illegal Migrant Work
articles.excerpt: To the outside world, Brunei, the tiny Southeast Asian monarchy, looks like a Shangri-La. The country, with a population of less than half a million, has one of the highest levels of GDP per capita in the world. Its benevolent Sultan has ensured free healthcare and education and highly subsidized food and housing for his subjects. There is no income tax. Brunei has the highest per capita car ownership in ASEAN – an average of two cars per household – and a high prevalence of foreign domestic workers, locally called “amah,” predominantly hailing from Indonesia and the Philippines. Given this background, the news of educated Bruneians going to Australia to work illegally on agricultural farms as fruit-pickers was shocking for someone who has worked in Brunei for 10 years. But a Reddit discussion on Brunei unemployment revealed that something is amiss in the Sultanate. Many unemployed people blamed foreign workers for taking their jobs in the private sector. For some, the easiest way out was Australia. The Bruneian passport, ranked 19th in the world, opens visa-free or visa-on-arrival access to 163 countries. The Electronic Travel Authority (ETA) gives a three-month tourist visa for just A$20. Although it is illegal for ETA holders to work, and if caught, the visa can be cancelled, for some desperate Bruneians the risk is worth taking, as A$30-A$50 per hour looks pretty good even after taking travel, board, and lodging into consideration. Although Australia has a program called the Working Holiday Maker (WHM) scheme, also called backpacker visa, which allows travelers to work during their stay to help finance their holiday, it comes with several caveats. There is generally a six-month limit on working for the same employer. More importantly, the scheme is available only to citizens of more than 40 partner countries and Brunei is not among them. This may explain why some Bruneians are using the ETA as a backdoor route to Australia in search of farm work.

articles.title: Taiwan’s Local Elections Are Not About China, President Lai, or the United States
articles.excerpt: This November, Taiwanese voters go to the polls to elect mayors, city councilors, and village chiefs. Many foreign policy observers will read the results as a verdict on Taiwanese attitudes toward China, President Lai Ching-te, Trump, or a potential war. That would be an analytical mistake. The outcomes cannot be explained by how voters feel about independence, unification, China, the United States, or any other national issue. As the saying goes, local elections are about local issues. Decades of data show that Taiwanese voters prioritize China, sovereignty, and Taiwan’s future in national elections, but we have little longitudinal data on how they decide in local ones. What we do know is that voters often cast ballots for mayor or city council differently than they do for president. For example, Taichung and New Taipei have elected a Kuomintang (KMT) mayor in each of the last two local elections, yet a majority of their voters still supported Lai and the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) in 2024. Electing a mayor from one party hardly means a city will back that party’s presidential candidate. Candidates across Taiwan are campaigning on local issues that vary by city, such as housing, public transportation, and urban renewal. Some touch on national issues, but most mayoral and city council candidates avoid them, since talking about national issues or polarizing figures could cost them votes. One telling example is the absence of both the DPP and KMT party leaders from most mayoral and city council election campaign advertisements. Lai, who is also the DPP chair, and KMT chair Cheng Li-wun are both deeply polarizing figures, specifically for their positions on national issues including China and Taiwan’s relationship with the United States. Featuring Lai or Cheng in a local campaign invites voters to see local candidates as extensions of their party’s divisive leadership rather than a local candidate.

articles.title: Japan and Australia: Toward a More Autonomous and Resilient Partnership
articles.excerpt: The security environment in the Indo-Pacific is undergoing a profound transformation. Cooperation among revisionist powers, including China, Russia, and North Korea, is deepening, while the strategic priorities of the United States — the country that has long underpinned the regional order — are also changing. At the same time, technological advances in areas such as artificial intelligence, autonomous systems, unmanned platforms, quantum technologies, and cyber capabilities are fundamentally changing the character of warfare and the sources of military advantage. Against this backdrop, Japan and Australia have deepened their comprehensive security partnership across military and economic domains. What matters increasingly is their ability to build both strategic autonomy and strategic resilience. Strategic autonomy does not mean “independence” from the United States. Rather, it means reducing excessive dependence on any single major power and preserving greater room for strategic choice and freedom of action. Strategic resilience, meanwhile, refers to the ability to withstand and recover from strategic shocks, whether they take the form of military conflict, economic coercion, supply-chain disruption, or energy crises. Together, these two concepts provide a useful framework for thinking about the current state and future direction of Japan–Australia cooperation. For much of the post-Cold War period, both Japan and Australia benefited from what might be called “dual dependence.” In security terms, both relied heavily on the United States, while economically they developed increasingly deep interdependence with China. This arrangement allowed them to enjoy security at relatively low defense costs while benefiting substantially from China’s economic growth. As U.S.–China rivalry and broader great-power competition intensify, however, this model is becoming increasingly difficult to sustain.

articles.title: Time for ASEAN to Revive its Customs Union Vision
articles.excerpt: As tariffs once again become bargaining tools for major powers, one of ASEAN’s key weaknesses is the fragmentation of its market across national tariff regimes. The revival of the Common External Tariff (CET) proposal, rejected four decades ago, raises a fundamental question: can ASEAN move beyond a mere “collection of assembly hubs” to become a higher-value-added economic region and a negotiating actor in its own right? A Customs Union Proposal Rejected 40 Years Ago ASEAN’s economic integration has been built on the ASEAN Free Trade Area (AFTA), agreed in 1992 and implemented through the Common Effective Preferential Tariff (CEPT) scheme from 1993. The CEPT lowered intra-ASEAN tariffs on goods originating in the region. A CET, by contrast, would require member states to apply a common external tariff schedule to imports from outside ASEAN. Its adoption would take ASEAN beyond a free trade area and towards a customs union. The CET is not a new idea. In August 1986, exactly 40 years ago, the Philippines, then ASEAN chair, proposed a customs union at the ASEAN Economic Ministers’ Meeting. The proposal called for intra-regional tariffs to be reduced gradually within a fixed time frame and for a common tariff to be imposed on imports from outside ASEAN. No consensus emerged: Indonesia opposed the deadline, while Singapore objected that the proposal could result in higher external tariffs. Intra-ASEAN trade then accounted for only about 20 percent of member states’ total trade, and their heavy dependence on external markets made a CET difficult to accept. AFTA’s Success—and the Borders That Remain ASEAN instead chose AFTA. This flexible form of integration eliminated most intra-regional tariffs while preserving each member state’s discretion over external tariffs. It supported ASEAN’s model of open regionalism – welcoming foreign investment and imported intermediate inputs while producing for global markets – and helped expand regional production networks.

articles.title: Russia’s Navy Shows Its Reach Around Japan’s Southwestern Islands
articles.excerpt: President Vladimir Putin’s mid-August visit to the Kuril Islands, his first as Russia’s leader, inflamed a decades-old territorial dispute with Japan and drew worldwide attention to the two countries’ border in the northern Pacific. But over the past several years, Russian forces have been increasingly active far to the south, around Japan’s southwestern-most islands, in a demonstration of the Russian military’s reach and its willingness to challenge its rivals on its own and alongside China. The dispute centers on the southernmost islands in the Kuril chain, which Japan calls its Northern Territories and says the Soviets seized illegally after Tokyo’s surrender at the end of World War II. Thousands of former Japanese residents of the islands are still alive, and resolving the dispute is a high priority for Japanese leaders. Russia’s activity on the islands, especially its military buildup, is therefore a sensitive issue for Tokyo. Putin’s visit to the island Russia calls Iturup and Japan calls Etorofu on August 13 struck a chord with Tokyo not only for its location but also for its timing. Putin first traveled to Sakhalin Island – his first visit there in 13 years – to observe drills by Russia’s Pacific Fleet, part of a month-long series of exercises in the area that Japan protested. His visit also came days after the anniversary of the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki and days before the anniversary of Japan’s World War II surrender announcement. Putin’s Kuril visit coincided with another Russian movement much farther south. The same day, Japan’s Defense Ministry reported that it had observed a Russian navy Improved Kilo-class submarine and a search-and-rescue vessel sailing north between the two Japanese islands closest to Taiwan, Yonaguni and Iriomote. That was one of at least 14 transits by Russian vessels around Yonaguni so far in 2026, a considerable increase over recent years.

articles.title: ‘A Tower of Jelly’
articles.excerpt: “What is the use of a fire brigade which vanishes from the scene as soon as the first smoke and flames appear?” asked Abba Eban, addressing an emergency session of the United Nations General Assembly soon after the 1967 Arab-Israeli War had ended. In a fiery speech, the foreign minister of Israel lashed out at the U.N. for pulling peacekeeping troops out of the Sinai Peninsula and the Gaza Strip. The “disastrously swift” withdrawal, Eban argued, had endangered the “national survival” of the Jewish state. Israel’s Six-Day War was nevertheless a spectacular military success. The Israel Defense Forces neutralized three Arab armies (Egypt, Jordan, and Syria) within a week and occupied the Sinai Peninsula, the Gaza Strip, the West Bank, East Jerusalem, and the Golan Heights. In his latest book, “Peacemaker,” historian Thant Myint-U offers new insights on the U.N.’s role in the events leading up to the six-day conflict. The book’s title refers to U Thant, the author’s grandfather. As U.N. secretary-general, the Burmese diplomat was the chief “firefighter” charged with deploying peacekeeping troops to conflict zones. The “most successful peacekeeping operation” was UNEF (United Nations Emergency Force), which had maintained a fragile peace along the border between Egypt and Israel for more than a decade. When the Egyptian military sent the U.N. an informal communication in mid-May requesting a withdrawal of peacekeeping troops, Thant faced a dilemma. Denying Cairo’s request would violate Egypt’s sovereignty, but removing the forces might jeopardize the U.N.’s conflict-prevention mission. The Secretary-General acquiesced after receiving an official letter from the foreign minister. However, as Thant was negotiating UNEF’s exit, Israeli jets strafed a convoy in the Egyptian-administered Gaza Strip, killing three soldiers.

articles.title: Indonesian President Replaces Foreign Minister With Career Diplomat
articles.excerpt: Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto has replaced his foreign minister with a career diplomat, in a cabinet reshuffle that saw more than a dozen other posts change hands. In yesterday’s reshuffle, Prabowo appointed Arrmanatha Nasir, Indonesia’s former permanent representative to ‌the United Nations in New York, as the country’s new foreign minister. The outgoing foreign minister, Sugiono, was shifted to the post of coordinating minister for human development. In this latest change to his “Red and White Cabinet,” Prabowo appointed three new coordinating ministers and a new minister of industry. He also reshuffled a handful of deputy ministerial posts and leadership positions at major government agencies, including the National Police and the office of the Ombudsman. The changeover at the top of Kemlu, however, was the most significant position to change hands, and the second major cabinet change ​in the past few weeks. In mid-September, Prabowo removed his finance minister, Purbaya Yudhi Sadewa and replaced him with ​his deputy, Suahasil Nazara, amid growing investor concern about Indonesia’s economic trajectory. Arrmanatha Nasir comes to the post with years of experience, having joined Kemlu in 1997. Since then, he has risen through the ranks, serving as the Ministry’s spokesperson between 2014 and 2019, Indonesia’s ambassador to France (2019-2021) and Indonesia’s ambassador to the U.N. (2021-2024). He was then appointed vice foreign minister when Prabowo took office. After taking his oath of office yesterday, Arrmanatha said that his priorities included “maintaining ​stability in the region and promoting multilateralism,” Reuters reported. Arrmanatha’s advent is likely to mark a significant change in the process of Indonesian foreign policymaking. His predecessor Sugiono was a political novice who came to the post with little hands-on experience in foreign affairs.

articles.title: Can Kashmir Learn From India’s Gen Z Movement?
articles.excerpt: On August 14, Jammu and Kashmir Chief Minister Omar Abdullah warned New Delhi of a potential Gen Z protest in the restive Himalayan region, while cataloguing the lieutenant governor’s endless attritions against his government – most recently the stalling on a reservation report that seeks to redress grievances over the open-merit category. On September 2, Abdullah’s Cabinet ministers descended onto Srinagar’s streets. Placards in hands, which named in bold, black letters the Narendra Modi regime’s repeated political incursions in Kashmir, they marched toward the headquarters of the Bharatiya Janata Party, the Hindu-nationalist party Modi heads. The demonstration was scuppered within minutes, with the police, which reports to the lieutenant governor, dashing on them. After a scuffle, the ministers were shoved inside vans like common criminals. Scores of television crews and YouTubers captured the excess, but no outrage followed on India’s primetime television that evening. Protest in Modi’s India rarely finds coverage on TV, except when it spirals out of control, like it did during the farmers’ march to Delhi in 2020-2021, or this summer’s Gen Z outburst over medical entrance test paper leaks. But that is less coverage and more of salvage job for the government. Media coverage often seems designed to provoke anger against the protesters, who are almost always depicted as foreign funded and scheming to weaken the country’s territorial integrity. The dismantling of the idea of protest painfully and saliently stirs the question: how, then, does one keep a republic? This was a basic question asked by American Founding Father Benjamin Franklin. In 1789, when asked whether the Constitutional Convention had resulted in a republic or a monarchy, Franklin famously responded: “A republic, if you can keep it.” But Franklin had reason for optimism.

articles.title: As University of Tokyo Gets Its First Female President, How Far Is Japan From Gender Equality?
articles.excerpt: On September 28, 2026, Fujigaki Yuko was selected as the next president of the University of Tokyo. Following formal appointment by the minister of education, culture, sports, science, and technology, she will take office on April 1, 2027, for a six-year term. As the university marks its 150th anniversary, Fujigaki will become the first woman to lead it. Yet at the institution she is about to head, only about one in five undergraduates is a woman. Fujigaki is not Japan’s first female university president. In 1997, Niwa Masako became president of Nara Women’s University, the first woman to head a national university in Japan, and in 2001, Honda Masuko became the first female president of Ochanomizu University. Coeducational national universities also have earlier precedents: Ikehata Setsuho became the first female president of Tokyo University of Foreign Studies in 2001, and Kina Ikue became the first female president of the University of the Ryukyus in 2025. Even so, the appointment of a woman to lead the University of Tokyo, often seen as Japan’s most prominent university and an institution with considerable social influence, carries particular symbolic weight. The Selection Process Fujigaki, 64, is a professor at the University of Tokyo’s Graduate School of Arts and Sciences, specializing in science and technology studies and scientometrics. She earned her bachelor’s, master’s, and doctoral degrees at the same university, completing her doctorate in 1990. Apart from nearly four years as a senior researcher at the government’s National Institute of Science and Technology Policy, she has spent her career at the university, becoming a professor in 2010. Starting in 2021, she served for five years as an executive vice president, overseeing areas including admissions, student support, and research ethics. Her selection has nevertheless generated controversy both inside and outside the university.

articles.title: Why Are Modi Government Critics Now Targeting India’s Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar?
articles.excerpt: “You must have heard of Dharmendra Pradhan,” student leader Neha Bora said in a video message on September 30, two days before a series of agitations is scheduled to start in major Indian cities like Delhi, Mumbai, and Kolkata, demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation. “Gyanesh Kumar, it’s your turn now. We are coming,” Bora said with a cheeky smile. A leftist student leader, Bora was part of the youth agitation in July that forced the Narendra Modi government’s education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan, out of office. Now, students and youth are rallying around the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) and opposition parties against a new target: Gyanesh Kumar, who has been at the center of political controversies since his appointment as chief election commissioner about a year and a half ago. Kumar has been accused of speaking political language and giving undue advantage to India’s ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). He is being compared with Adolf Eichmann, the central operational manager of the Holocaust. The latest trigger for the nationwide protests that will begin on October 2 was an investigation by The Indian Express, which reported that two members of the Election Commission, Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi, had raised concerns with Kumar at least 14 times in 10 months, only to be overlooked. Some decisions were reportedly taken without their knowledge. The objections concerned electoral roll decisions and orders. Notably, Kumar is the first chief election commissioner appointed under a new law that the Modi government brought, overturning a mechanism recommended by India’s Supreme Court. This new law gives the government the authority to pick election commissioners of its choice. The law also gives immunity to the election commissioner for any action they take with regard to conducting elections.

articles.title: China’s Stake in the Russian Duma Elections
articles.excerpt: What did observers in China think about the Russian State Duma election on September 20? While retaining a veneer of democratic procedure, Vladimir Putin has steadily eliminated potential rivals and term limits, much like Xi Jinping has done. In past Russian election cycles, Chinese officials and experts by large have emphasized the importance of outcomes reinforcing political stability in Russia. In terms of the latest election, most Western commentary criticized the unfair process preventing Putin’s primary opposing party, Yabloko, from running. Yabloko – which means apple in Russian but actually is an acronym for the last names of its three founders – is the only pro-democracy and anti-war party in Russia. By contrast, China’s Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun congratulated Russia for the “smooth conclusion” of the process and hailed the elections for representing “the will of the Russian people.” Chinese media commentary did note that Yabloko was prohibited from participating in the election as a party, although some Yabloko candidates were still running in single-member districts (and all lost). Given the lack of real electoral competition, a Hong Kong media outlet, China Review News Agency, pointed out that the 59 percent turnout (7.6 percentage points higher than the previous Duma election in 2021) reflected “the state’s mobilization capabilities,” not increased political participation. Putin’s televised address in the lead-up to the election framed it as an opportunity for Russians to express their support for the war in Ukraine and as “a collective response to those who seek to weaken Russia,” Chinese commentary reported. More than 200 Russian veterans of the war in Ukraine ran for the Duma and election commission chair Ella Pamfilova reported that 46 of them won seats – 41 of whom belonged to United Russia, the ruling party that has dominated the Russian political landscape throughout Putin’s leadership.

articles.title: Taiwan Can’t Fight Beijing’s History War While Erasing Its Own ROC Legacy
articles.excerpt: At last week’s summit between U.S. President Donald Trump and China’s President Xi Jinping, the White House described the United States and China as World War II allies who “fought side by side to win the war.” It was a small phrase with a large omission. The government that represented China during the war, and fought alongside the United States against Japan, was the Republic of China (ROC). The government Xi leads – the People’s Republic of China (PRC) – did not exist until 1949, four years after Japan’s surrender. By collapsing the two into a single, unbroken “China,” the summit’s language risked allowing the PRC to inherit the legacy of a war it did not fight. Taiwan’s government noticed. Its Mainland Affairs Council pushed back, insisting that the ROC was the “true ally” that fought with the United States during the war, and emphasizing that the PRC did not even exist during World War II. Deputy Foreign Minister Wu Chih-chung went further, calling the framing an act of “de-ROC-ization” – in which the Republic of China’s very existence is being erased from history, and replaced by the Chinese Communist Party. “We should feel very distressed,” Wu added. Taiwanese scholars echoed the concern, warning that if Washington adopts Beijing’s version of events, the result could be a further hollowing out of the ROC’s place in the historical record. There is an obvious irony in Taipei’s complaint, however. Taiwan’s government has been taking steps to distance itself from the ROC moniker. This year, Taiwan’s representative office in Los Angeles sent out National Day invitations branded “Taiwan National Day.” The previous year’s cards had read “Republic of China 114th National Day.” The same government whose deputy foreign minister accused Beijing of erasing the ROC internationally was removing references to the ROC from its own diplomatic correspondence. This trend also impacts how Taiwan’s government speaks about World War II.

articles.title: Australia as an AI Middle Power
articles.excerpt: Australia’s role in the frontier world of artificial intelligence was the focus in Canberra last month, with two events bringing together hundreds of defense, diplomacy, development, and industry experts. The Australian Strategic Policy Institute (ASPI) gathered the national security and defense community for an AI Masterclass on September 14. The next day, the Development Intelligence Lab’s Situation 2026 explored how AI can solve Indo-Pacific development challenges. The events revealed a country grappling with what it means to be a middle power in the age of AI. As ClearAI founder Jisoo Kim put it, at a time when AI is developing at breakneck speed and reordering economies and societies, “Where in this ecosystem, where in this global economy is Australia going to sit?” Judging from opinion polling, many Australians would probably prefer that AI had never been invented. But now that the cat is out of the bag, Australia needs to think about what it means for its security and prosperity, and the risks and opportunities it brings. As a middle power, with a range of assets and resources, Australia is not powerless in the face of these changes. It has some capacity to influence the new world that AI is making. Assistant Minister for the Digital Economy Andrew Charlton addressed this openly. Asking how middle powers manage AI, he identified four plays: alignment with a superpower, leverage in the value chain, competition through different models and capabilities, and sovereign capability. Charlton stated that Australia is pursuing all four simultaneously. Shadow Minister for Industry and Sovereign Capability Andrew Hastie broadly agreed, particularly emphasizing the U.S. relationship as Australia’s “line to sovereignty.” Hastie suggested using Australia’s relationships in Washington to encourage a hyperscaler to invest in Australia.

articles.title: The New Development Bank Quietly Delivers During India’s BRICS Year
articles.excerpt: As India hosted the BRICS summit in New Delhi in September 2026, a familiar question returned: does the grouping produce anything beyond summit statements? The New Development Bank (NDB) offers the clearest evidence in the affirmative. India first proposed the bank at an earlier BRICS summit in New Delhi in 2012, and its 2026 chairship of BRICS brought that idea full circle. Judging a development bank is not simple; big announcements matter less than the money that actually reaches projects. The NDB’s record can thus be evaluated on three broad counts. The first is how much it has lent and how much of that money has actually been paid out. The second is whom the bank lends to. The third is how it raises the money it lends. On all three, the picture is more encouraging than the NDB’s low public profile suggests. By the end of June 2026, the NDB had approved loans worth about $44 billion for 141 projects in clean energy, transport, water systems and digital infrastructure. Of that amount, roughly $25 billion had already been paid out to borrowers. The second figure is especially important. Many development banks approve large loans but pay out much less, and much more slowly. A bank that has paid out more than half of what it approved is doing real work, not just signing agreements. The NDB’s public figures show what this money is building: 2,400 megawatts of clean energy capacity under way, 1,400 kilometers of tunnels and canals, 43 schools built or upgraded and a large increase in sewage treatment capacity. The bank’s reach has also grown. Its founding members were Brazil, Russia, India, China, and South Africa. It has since added Algeria, Bangladesh, Egypt, the United Arab Emirates, and Uzbekistan. Its members now stretch from South and Central Asia to Africa, the Middle East, and Latin America. India’s place in the NDB is unusual. It helped create the bank, it owns an equal share of it, and it is one of its biggest borrowers.

articles.title: Iran War Highlights 2 Challenges for Japan in a Taiwan Contingency
articles.excerpt: On February 28, the Iran-U.S. war began. Despite ongoing negotiations between the United States and Iran at the time, Israel and the U.S. launched a barrage of attacks, and Iran retaliated across a wide area, including Israel and the Gulf region. In the Strait of Hormuz, attacks on commercial vessels, heightened vigilance against mines and drones, traffic control measures, and a U.S. maritime blockade of Iran combined to impose severe constraints on shipping routes that are vital to global energy transportation. Even in late September, traffic through the strait had not returned to prewar levels, and the crisis had yet to be fully resolved. Against this backdrop, Japan can use the Iran war to reexamine its security framework, with particular attention to preparations for a contingency involving Taiwan. The Iran war has raised many issues, but two are especially important for Japan. The first is how to evacuate Japanese nationals and travelers when a crisis begins sooner than expected and civilian transportation networks suddenly cease to function. The second is how Japan can help ensure the safety of maritime traffic while avoiding becoming a direct party to the conflict. Both expose gaps in the institutional arrangements Japan has developed with a Taiwan contingency in mind. Evacuating People from a Sudden Crisis The first lesson of the Iran war is that the traditional approach of waiting until a crisis escalates before evacuating people is no longer sufficient. Even before the outbreak of hostilities, the Japanese government had warned of the deteriorating situation in Iran and encouraged Japanese nationals to leave early. Once the fighting began, however, it became necessary to confirm the safety of Japanese nationals and assist with their departure not only in Iran but also across neighboring areas, including Israel, Qatar, Bahrain, and the United Arab Emirates.

articles.title: Central Asia’s Diplomatic Balancing Act on Display from Bishkek to New York
articles.excerpt: The general debate of the 81st U.N. General Assembly closed this week, and the Central Asian speeches put the region’s balancing act on full display. As the world moves toward multipolarity, the five Central Asian states find themselves in a tight spot. They must manage relations with the two leading global powers, the United States and China, while preserving their ties with Russia, with which they share deep historical, economic, and political bonds. Three weeks before the debate opened, Kyrgyzstan hosted the Shanghai Cooperation Organization’s (SCO) 25th-anniversary summit on August 31 and September 1. Four of the five Central Asian states – Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, and Uzbekistan – are SCO members, while neutral Turkmenistan remains formally out, although it occasionally participates as a guest. The SCO is widely seen as a vehicle for Beijing and Moscow to limit Washington’s footprint in Eurasia, and the 2026 summit’s Bishkek Declaration gave the United States plenty to dislike, from a firm condemnation of military strikes on Iran to opposition to “unilateral coercive measures.” Taken together, the two gatherings reveal a clear division of labor in Central Asian diplomacy. The region’s governments echo Beijing’s and Moscow’s grievances in regional group settings like the SCO, court Washington with concrete deals via bilateral channels, and use the U.N. General Assembly (UNGA) podium to say as little as possible that might offend any of the three. The balancing starts with who showed up. Presidents Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, Emomali Rahmon, Shavkat Mirziyoyev, and Sadyr Japarov all attended the SCO summit in person, alongside China’s Xi Jinping, Russia’s Vladimir Putin, and India’s Narendra Modi. Three weeks later, only Japarov traveled to New York, after making a stop in the U.S. state of Utah. All five Central Asian countries had sent their heads of state last year for the U.N.’s 80th anniversary.

articles.title: Officials Detained as Kazakhstan Mourns Soldiers Perished at Sea
articles.excerpt: Crossroads Asia | Security | Central Asia Five military officials were arrested in connection to the deaths of 14 servicemen lost at sea during a combat exercise in southwestern Kazakhstan, as a day of national mourning is observed. Kazakhstan is mourning the deaths of 14 servicemen who were lost during a military drill. The tragedy took place on September 24 during the 2026 Caspian Defense exercise in southwestern Kazakhstan. The episode has led to the dismissal of the defense minister, while five officials are being investigated for negligence in relation to the case. According to the Kazakh Ministry of Defense, a total of 17 servicemen were swept out to sea during one of the naval exercises due to a sudden deterioration in weather in the area, including strong winds. While rescue teams did manage to save three servicemen, the remainder were lost, their bodies recovered over the following days. While President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev declared a day of mourning out of respect for the soldiers who passed away, criticism has hit the authorities hard, both regarding the accident and the subsequent approach by the authorities to the relatives of the deceased. The accidental deaths prompted criticism at all levels of authority, not least in regards to how the tragedy was communicated to the relatives who were left behind. As news about the September 24 accident spread, relatives of servicemen involved in the exercise started to gather outside the Aktau morgue located close to the scene of the accident. There they sought answers regarding who was lost, demanding the names of those who had been identified. Separated by a fence surrounding the morgue, military personnel later that day read out the names of the identified servicemen, most of whom were under the age of 25.

articles.title: The Lingering Shadow of Rodrigo Duterte’s Drug War in the Philippines
articles.excerpt: A few bags of chips and sweets line the modest storefront of Salvacion Ramos’ home in the Batasan neighborhood on the outskirts of Manila. At 68, she has turned the front of her house into a small convenience store to help pay for the education of her grandson, who has been in her care since her daughter’s death. It was on that same doorstep one night in February 2017 that Cristeta Ramos was shot once in the back and three times in the head by four plainclothes police officers. “She died in my arms. I didn’t even get to say goodbye,” Salvacion recalls, tears in her eyes. Beside her, her friend and neighbor Llore Pasco is also mourning her children. Her two sons, Cristanto and Juan Carlos, 34 and 31, were killed during a police operation as they were on their way to work in May 2017. “The police say they chased them because they thought they were thieves, but the bullet wounds were on the front of their bodies,” Llore says. She is now raising her five grandchildren. “Cristeta was not a criminal” Salvacion says. “She did take drugs with the people she was with, but she wanted to get better. The barangay [neighborhood-level community] was offering a program for drug users to seek treatment, so I gave them her name.” Llore’s sons had stopped using drugs well before Duterte’s election. After he took office, local officials insisted that former drug users register, presenting the process as a simple verification. Her sons initially refused. Llore eventually convinced them. They had been sober for more than a year. “Today I keep thinking that if they had not gone there, they might still be alive,” she says. In neighborhoods across the country, barangays began compiling “watch lists” of current and former drug users. For some residents, getting off those lists came at a price. “At least five families I know paid 10,000 pesos (about $180) to the local government to get their names removed from the list, and their children are still alive,” Salvacion says.

articles.title: The Woman Who Held Mahathir’s Hand For 70 Years
articles.excerpt: ASEAN Beat | Society | Southeast Asia Siti Hasmah Mohamad Ali, who died this week aged 100, was a close companion of Mahathir throughout his long and tumultuous political career. Former Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad and his wife Siti Hasmah Mohamad Ali attend Mahathir’s 100th birthday celebration at the Perdana Leadership Foundation in Putrajaya, Malaysia, July 10, 2025. Credit: Wikimedia Commons/Jackie Wee Dr. Siti Hasmah Mohamad Ali had just one complaint about her husband, Dr. Mahathir Mohamad: that he was very shy about holding her hand in public. The man, who remained loyal and faithful to her for more than 70 years, felt a little embarrassed about showing his love for the Malay girl he met at King Edward VII College of Medicine in Singapore in 1947. On Mahathir’s 93rd birthday, in an interview with Channel NewsAsia conducted by 10-year-old Kashika Selvam, Siti Hasmah narrated a funny incident about holding hands. She said that he was so shy that once, while driving through a highway toll booth, he pulled back his hand because he didn’t want the toll operator to see them holding hands. Mahathir ruled Malaysia ruthlessly between 1981 and 2003, during which his critics and detractors were the subjects of sometimes furious political vendettas. But when it comes to his fidelity and faithfulness to Siti Hasmah, even his critics cannot raise a finger against him. At home, Mahathir was a loyal husband and an affectionate father, thanks in large part to Siti Hasmah. His daughter, Marina Mahathir, says her mother insisted that the siblings show their love and affection for each other openly by hugging and kissing. Unlike many other politicians’ wives, Siti Hasmah’s conduct in public never gave a hint that she was the prime minister’s wife. Narrating a poignant incident in the 2019 documentary “M for Malaysia,” Siti Hasmah says: “I was taking my husband to the hospital, not the Prime Minister of Malaysia,” when Mahathir suffered a heart attack in 1989.

articles.title: Can Myanmar’s New Administration Revive the Stalled Dawei SEZ Project?
articles.excerpt: Myanmar’s military-backed administration is again trying to put the long-stalled Dawei Special Economic Zone (SEZ) project on the agenda. This time, Russia has emerged as a potential partner for some of its port and energy plans, but it remains unclear whether it can turn the area into a functioning economic zone. The Dawei SEZ, with its proposed deep-sea port, sits on Myanmar’s Andaman coast. It faces the Indian Ocean and has an overland connection to Thailand and the wider Mekong region. The 138-kilometer-long Dawei-Htee Khee road, opened in 2013 but still requiring major upgrades, could connect the SEZ to the Southern Economic Corridor through Bangkok, Phnom Penh, and Ho Chi Minh City. For Thailand and the wider Mekong, Dawei could offer a westward route to the Indian Ocean that bypasses the Strait of Malacca. This position has long underpinned the project’s strategic and economic significance. Dawei was an ambitious project from the beginning. Launched in 2008 under Myanmar’s military regime, it combined a deep-sea port, an industrial estate, power generation and utilities, and a road link across the border to Thailand. The early estimates for the entire project exceeded $50 billion. However, financial and development problems led to major restructuring in 2015–16, during Myanmar’s democratic transition. The challenge was raising enough capital and moving different parts of the project forward together. The industrial zone needed power, water, transport, and access to a seaport. The port, in turn, relied on cargo and industrial activity. Investors also needed confidence that the wider infrastructure would be built. Much of Dawei’s regional potential also rested on having a reliable connection to Thailand. Yet the Dawei-Htee Khee road on the Myanmar side was poorly suited to serve as a major industrial corridor. Limited border facilities and cargo transfer capacity created additional bottlenecks.

articles.title: UN Refugee Agency Expresses Concerns About Malaysia’s Deportation of Asylum Seekers to Myanmar
articles.excerpt: The United Nations refugee agency yesterday expressed its concerns over Malaysia’s return this week of nearly 1,500 asylum seekers to Myanmar, in spite of the ongoing conflict and dire humanitarian situation inside the country. The 1,476 people were returned to Myanmar via ship on Tuesday, the first phase in the agreed “voluntary” repatriation of some 5,000 asylum seekers currently held in Malaysian immigration detention centers. While Malaysia insists that the returns are strictly voluntary, the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) said yesterday that it was concerned about the fate of the 1,476 people, given the country’s continuing conflict and dire human rights and humanitarian situation. Since those returned had been held in detention centers, it had “serious questions about whether decisions to return were genuinely free and informed,” UNHCR Assistant High Commissioner for Protection Edem Wosornu said in a statement. The U.N. agency has been blocked from accessing Malaysian immigration detention centers since 2019. “We are concerned by these returns at a time when people sent back to Myanmar may face serious risks, and some within the group may be in need of international protection,” Wosornu said. While recognizing Malaysia’s “sovereign responsibility” to manage asylum and migration issues, UNHCR urged the government “to ensure that all returns are subject to robust safeguards, including individual assessments and access to protection procedures.” UNHCR’s statement came as Malaysia’s government confirmed that 3,524 refugees had been approved for the second phase of the “voluntary repatriation program.” Communications Minister Fahmi Fadzil said yesterday that the individuals had been identified by the Myanmar authorities, and that their names were submitted to Malaysia in a diplomatic note dated August 13. He added that Kuala Lumpur was awaiting notification from Myanmar on the date for the repatriation.

articles.title: China’s Military Open New Logistics and Training Facility in Laos
articles.excerpt: This week, the Chinese military opened a new logistics and training facility at an airport in Laos, further expanding its regional security presence and establishing the first overseas presence of the Chinese air force. In a statement, China’s Ministry of Defense said that the China-Laos Military Joint Support and Training Center was inaugurated on Tuesday, in a ceremony that was attended by Lao Defense Minister Khamlieng Outhakaysone and a delegation from the Chinese People’s Liberation Army (PLA). The facility, which is based at Ban Keun Airport, which sits close to the Nam Ngum River around 50 kilometers north of the capital Vientiane, also includes a China-Laos Friendship Aviation Academy. “The center, jointly maintained and operated by both sides, is aimed at helping Laos strengthen the training of its air force pilots,” the Ministry said, but offered no details about what personnel or equipment would be based at the airport. “The construction and use of the center reflect mutual respect and equal consultation between China and Laos, comply with both countries’ domestic laws, relevant international law and common practice,” it said. “It is not directed against any third party and contributes to enhancing practical military cooperation as well as promoting regional peace and stability.” Satellite imagery of the Ban Keun facility shows it also includes the construction of an extensive airfield. According to Reuters, work began on the new airfield in late 2025 and work was ongoing as of early September. “In place of green fields,” it reported, “a large paved runway and a parallel taxiway and apron were visible, along with a number of new buildings.” The airport was built on the site of an airfield known as Lima Site 44, one of a network of airstrips that were used by the U.S. military and Central Intelligence Agency during the Vietnam War, when the U.S. secretly supported an insurgency by anti-communist Hmong rebels.

articles.title: Japan Has Been Here Before: The 1987 Persian Gulf Crisis
articles.excerpt: The Strait of Hormuz was effectively closed following the U.S. and Israeli attacks on Iran in February, leaving oil tankers unable to transit the strait, which is both the entrance to the Persian Gulf and one of the world’s most critical trade arteries. Japan imports more than 90 percent of its crude oil from the Middle East. Gasoline prices have surged, and the effects on daily life have been wide-ranging. The current crisis has a precedent. During the Iran-Iraq War of the 1980s, the Japanese government actively debated whether to send Maritime Self-Defense Force (MSDF) minesweepers and Japan Coast Guard (JCG) patrol vessels to the Persian Gulf — and ultimately chose not to. Iraq invaded Iran in September 1980, beginning the Iran–Iraq War. Around 1984 the conflict spread to the sea, and passage through the Persian Gulf became hazardous for tankers as missile attacks and mines proliferated. In July 1987, at Kuwait’s request, the U.S. government dispatched warships and began escorting tankers, but a tanker still struck a mine. Washington then asked Western countries, including Japan, to send minesweepers. The U.K., France, Italy, the Netherlands, and Belgium all subsequently contributed to the minesweeping effort. The Japanese government began exploring how it could contribute to navigational safety in the Gulf. Prime Minister Nakasone Yasuhiro was personally in favor of deploying personnel via MSDF minesweepers. On August 27, 1987, speaking before a Lower House committee, he argued that while he did not intend to order the dispatch, the act of removing mines would not, in his view, constitute the use of force, and that sending vessels to the Persian Gulf would not constitute the overseas dispatch of troops. Naval mines constitute weapons of naval warfare, and laying them is an established means of naval combat. Under international law, minesweeping operations conducted during an armed conflict are themselves considered a use of force.

articles.title: Who Is Russia’s New Ambassador to North Korea?
articles.excerpt: Russia has finally filled the ambassadorial post in Pyongyang, which had sat vacant for nearly eight months. Under a decree signed by President Vladimir Putin on July 28, career diplomat Andrei Podelyshev – at the time, Russia’s ambassador to Nigeria, a post he had held since December 2024 – was named the new ambassador extraordinary and plenipotentiary to the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea. A companion decree released him from his Nigerian posting the same day. Podelyshev arrived in Pyongyang nearly two months later, on September 26, together with his wife, aboard a direct Nordwind flight from Moscow. According to the Russian Embassy and TASS, he headed straight from the airport to the Soviet-era Liberation Monument to pay tribute to fallen Red Army soldiers, before visiting Pyongyang’s newly built memorial complex for North Korean troops killed fighting alongside Russian forces in Kursk. Podelyshev is, on paper, one of the more genuinely “Korea-literate” diplomats Moscow could have sent. He graduated from MGIMO (the Moscow State Institute of International Relations) in 1984 and joined the Soviet Foreign Ministry that same year. He speaks both English and Korean, and over his career he has served at the Soviet embassy in Pyongyang itself, as well as at Russian missions in South Korea and the United States. What stands out, though, is the decade he spent away from Asia desks entirely. From 2005 to 2015, Podelyshev was deputy director of the Consular Department of the Russian Foreign Ministry, the branch of the ministry responsible for visas, citizenship matters, and the movement of foreign nationals in and out of Russia. That background is not a minor biographical footnote. Consular policy has become one of the most sensitive, and most scrutinized, levers of the entire North Korea-Russia relationship.

articles.excerpt: A moins de sept mois de la présidentielle 2027, les cinq candidats à la primaire sociale-démocrate se sont réunis sur BFM-TV dans un format « Vous président », animé par Apolline de Malherbe et Maxime Switek, visant à convaincre les indécis, cinq jours avant le premier tour. Live animé par Minh Dréan, Louise Vallée et Audrey Delaporte © AGNÈS DHERBEYS/MYOP POUR «LE MONDE» 00:26 C’est la fin de ce live ! Merci à tous et toutes de l’avoir suivi. Vous pouvez retrouver l’ensemble des sujets sur la primaire à gauche – dont le premier tour se tiendra les 9 et 10 octobre et le second les 16 et 17 octobre – mais aussi plus largement sur la présidentielle en cliquant ici. Le 05/10 à 00:25 L’essentiel Ce qu’il faut retenir du dernier débat entre les candidats à la primaire sociale-démocrate A cinq jours du premier tour, et alors que les adhésions pour participer à la primaire seront clôturées lundi soir, Ségolène Royal, Emmanuel Maurel, Jérôme Guedj, Raphaël Glucksmann et Olivier Faure se sont retrouvés pour un dernier débat, dimanche soir sur BFM-TV. Après s’être − une nouvelle fois − déchirés au sujet de la question des alliances avec La France insoumise, que Raphaël Glucksmann et Jerôme Guedj refusent catégoriquement, ainsi que sur les propos du candidat de Place publique diffusés par Le Média, ils ont débattu pendant plus de 3 heures, et répondu aux questions d’un panel d’électeurs indécis. Interrogés sur la mobilisation lycéenne, et l’appel des syndicats à soutenir le mouvement le 6 octobre, les candidats ont unanimement salué les revendications légitimes des élèves. « Ils doivent être entendus », a défendu Olivier Faure, dénonçant avec Jerôme Guedj la violence de la répression du mouvement par les forces de l’ordre. Chacun a défendu sa vision de la réforme des retraites.

articles.summary:
又一次只是平局。在尤尔根·克洛普的执教下，德国国家队在对阵希腊时未能取得进球，最终以0:0收场。从国际媒体的角度看，德国队的比赛在许多方面仍存在不足。以下是国际媒体的评论：

希腊《塔内亚报》：「对于国家队来说，这是一个重要的积分，他们在小组中保持不败，并梦想着进入四分之一决赛！」
《每日报》：「国家队在对阵德国时取得了一场宝贵的0:0平局。」

法国《队报》：「尤尔根·克洛普的德国队缺乏想象力，在希腊未能取得进球。上半场占据主导，下半场却显得迟缓。」

西班牙《马卡报》：「克洛普强调现在是实验的时候了。但到目前为止，他的德国队并没有真正进入状态。」
《世界体育报》：「尤尔根·克洛普的球队与一周前对阵希腊时排出了完全不同的首发阵容，他们从失利中吸取了教训，从一开始就占据主导，但他们的计划逐渐失败了。」
《阿斯报》：「克洛普时代没有启动。」

意大利《体育邮报》：「德国队体力不支，沃尔特马德在下半场被换上场。」

奥地利《皇冠报》：「平局！德国队错失了向希腊复仇的机会。」

瑞士《观察报》：「铁骨铮铮的希腊人再次让克洛普恼火。德国队在对阵希腊时未能取得进球。希腊人龟缩防守，用尽一切手段抵抗德国队球星。」

articles.title: RAF Fairford: US-Luftwaffe zieht alle Bomber nach Anschlagsverdacht ab
articles.excerpt: Im Fall des Luftwaffenstützpunkts Fairford (hier mehr) in Großbritannien gibt es bemerkenswerte Entwicklungen. Das Pentagon erklärte, dass sämtliche US-Langstreckenbomber abgezogen worden sind. »Wir können nun bestätigen, dass alle US-Bomber, die auf dem Stützpunkt RAF Fairford stationiert waren, wieder an ihre Heimatstützpunkte in den Vereinigten Staaten zurückgekehrt sind«, teilte ein Beamter des US-Verteidigungsministeriums auf Anfrage mit. Aus Gründen der operativen Sicherheit habe das Ressort zuvor »Bewegungen unserer Ressourcen und Streitkräfte nicht in Echtzeit« kommentieren können, hieß es weiter. Nach Informationen der »New York Times« waren neue Drohungen gegen den Militärstützpunkt der Grund für den überraschenden Abzug der US-Bomber. So gebe es Informationen über einen von Iran unterstützten Anschlag auf den Stützpunkt, berichtete die Zeitung unter Berufung auf zwei US-Beamte. Darauf angesprochen, wollte sich das Pentagon nicht weiter äußern. Den Angaben zufolge sagte ein US-Beamter, dass die Informationen zwar Teil jener Warnungen von vor drei Wochen seien. Die Lage habe sich in den vergangenen 24 Stunden allerdings aufgrund konkreter Details zugespitzt. Kontrollen vor der Luftwaffenbasis Fairford (am 28. September) Foto: Toby Shepheard / REUTERS Die US-Streitkräfte hatten im März weitere Langstreckenbomber nach Großbritannien verlegt, um so flexibler im Krieg gegen Iran agieren zu können. Im Rahmen der normalen Rotation waren laut US-Medien zahlreiche Bomber erst in der vergangenen Woche auf dem Stützpunkt eingetroffen – nun mussten sie ihn schon wieder verlassen. Nach Angaben der »»New York Times«» wurde die Notwendigkeit der Verlegung der Bomber weg von RAF Fairford als so dringlich eingestuft, dass einige Maschinen bereits starteten, während die benötigten Tankflugzeuge für die Unterstützung über dem Atlantik erst noch vorbereitet werden mussten.

articles.title: Israels Spieler tragen Armbinden in Gedenken an Terror-Opfer
articles.excerpt: Die israelische Fußball-Nationalmannschaft lief in Gedenken an die Opfer des Terrorangriffs der Hamas vom 7. Oktober 2023 beim Nations-League-Spiel am Abend gegen Irland mit schwarzen Armbinden und der Aufschrift »7.10« auf. Einen entsprechenden Antrag hatte die Europäische Fußball-Union UEFA genehmigt, wie der israelische Verband vor dem Anpfiff mitteilte.Am 7. Oktober 2023 hatten Kämpfer der Hamas und anderer extremistischer Organisationen rund 1200 Menschen in Israel getötet und mehr als 250 weitere als Geiseln nach Gaza verschleppt. Der beispiellose Überfall löste den Gaza-Krieg aus. Seitdem wurden nach Angaben der von der Hamas kontrollierten Gesundheitsbehörde im Gazastreifen mehr als 74.000 Palästinenser getötet. Seit Oktober 2025 herrscht im Gaza-Krieg eigentlich eine Waffenruhe, es gibt aber immer wieder tödliche Angriffe. Protestaktionen auch im HinspielDas Spiel im serbischen Backa Topola war auch deswegen brisant, weil es in Irland eine enorme Unterstützung für Palästina gibt. Wie schon beim Hinspiel-Duell im ungarischen Debrecen drückten die irischen Spieler auf unterschiedliche Weise ihren Protest aus. Sie waren mit schwarzen Armbinden aufgelaufen, bei der israelischen Hymne hielten sie ihre Köpfe gesenkt. Zudem gab es keinerlei Abklatschen vor dem Spiel, auch nicht bei der Seitenwahl.

articles.title: Cornell University: Anwalt berichtet von Drohungen gegen »Jane Doe«
articles.excerpt: Sie soll im Oktober 2024 unter Drogen gesetzt und anschließend über Stunden von mehreren Studenten der Eliteuni Cornell im US-Bundesstaat New York vergewaltigt worden sein. Nun wird die Frau, die diese Vorwürfe erhebt, nach Angaben ihres Anwalts zum Ziel von Drohungen. Thomas Giuffra, der die nur unter dem Pseudonym »Jane Dow« bekannte Frau vertritt, sagte im Sender CNN, ihr sei gedroht worden, sie zum Schweigen zu bringen oder ihr Schaden zuzufügen, sollte sie ihre Zivilklage nicht zurückziehen. »Sie hat zahlreiche Drohungen erhalten«, sagte Giuffra und fügte hinzu, auch er sei bedroht worden.»Ich habe keine Angst vor diesen Leuten«, sagte er. »Aber die Drohungen, die Beschimpfungen, um das, was vor sich geht, zu schützen, den Status quo – diese Typen sind widerlich. Sie sollten im Keller ihrer Mutter bleiben und sich aus der Welt heraushalten.« Am Samstag hatte Cornell-Präsident Michael Kotlikoff in einer Videobotschaft angekündigt, dass die Universität die Rolle von Studentenverbindungen auf dem Campus untersuchen werde. Anlass waren die heftigen Proteste, die es wegen des Umgangs der Hochschule mit den Vergewaltigungsvorwürfen gegeben hatte.»Im besten Fall können diese Organisationen den Studierenden Freundschaft, Zugehörigkeit, Mentoring und ein starkes Gemeinschaftsgefühl bieten«, sagte er und fügte hinzu: »Aber die Zugehörigkeit zu einer Gruppe kann niemals die individuelle Verantwortung mindern.«Unter anderem stehen die Staatsanwälte im Tompkins County des Bundesstaats New York wegen ihrer anfänglichen Behandlung der Vorwürfe in der Kritik. New Yorks Gouverneurin ernannte in der vergangenen Woche eine Sonderermittlerin, um den Fall zu untersuchen. US-Präsident Donald Trump, der James seit Jahren feindselig gegenübersteht, kritisierte ihre Ernennung scharf. »Ich habe Mitleid mit jedem, gegen den sie ermittelt, denn diese Person wird keine faire Behandlung erfahren«, sagte Trump am Freitag gegenüber Reportern.

articles.title: Alexander Karp: Palantir-Chef lässt 15.000 Hektar Wald in Schweden kaufen
articles.excerpt: Palantir-Gründer und CEO Alexander Karp hat in der schwedischen Provinz Härjedalen ein Waldgrundstück gekauft. Wie der schwedische Sender »SVT« unter Berufung auf die Lokalzeitung »Tidningen Härjedalen« berichtet, wurden in der Gemeinde Storsjö Kapell 15.000 Hektar Wald für umgerechnet 21 Millionen Euro an ein Unternehmen von Karp verkauft. Der Kauf erfolgte demnach über die Firma »Scandinavian Trust«, hinter der wiederum das neu gegründete Unternehmen »Cladonia Skog AB« steckt. Eigentümer von »Cladonia Skog AB« ist Alexander Karp.Jagdpächter verlieren JagdrechteBekannt wurde der Verkauf des Grundstücks, als lokale Jäger im Juni darüber benachrichtigt wurden, dass sie südlich von Storsjö Kapell ab Herbst nicht mehr jagen dürften. Die betroffenen Jäger zeigten sich gegenüber »Tidningen Härjedalen« verärgert darüber, fortan dort nicht mehr auf Elchjagd gehen zu können. Der Entzug der Jagdrechte erfolgte, nachdem der Papierhersteller »Svenska Cellulosa Aktiebolaget« (SCA) das Land an Karps »Scandinavian Trust« verkauft hatte. Die Kündigung der Jagdvereinbarung sei ein natürlicher Bestandteil des Verkaufsprozesses, teilte SCA mit. Außerdem hieß es, das Land sei aus forstwirtschaftlicher Sicht nicht optimal gewesen.»Das Land besteht größtenteils aus kahlen Bergen und Bergwäldern«, sagte ein Pressesprecher der SCA gegenüber dem Sender »SVT«. SCA teilte weiter mit: »Es handelt sich um einen Wald, der sich hervorragend für Erholung, Jagd, Skifahren und Wandern eignet – was, wie wir erfahren haben, auch der Hauptgrund für die Kaufentscheidung war.« Spekulationen über Nutzung des GrundstücksSeitdem der Verkauf bekannt wurde, kursiert die Spekulation, Karp könnte eine Rechenzentrum auf dem Grundstück bauen wollen. Auf eine Nachfrage des Sender »SVT« teilte »Scandinavian Trust« mit, der neue Eigentümer wolle das Waldgrundstück »mit großem Respekt vor der Natur und den schwedischen Traditionen« bewirtschaften.

articles.title: Bad Neuenahr-Ahrweiler: Unbekannter zerkratzt Autos und hinterlässt Nummer eine Frau
articles.excerpt: In Bad Neuenahr-Ahrweiler sind in der Nacht auf Sonntag mindestens 41 geparkte Autos beschädigt worden. Ein noch unbekannter Täter zerkratzte die Wagen nach Polizeiangaben mit einem spitzen Gegenstand und hinterließ teils Zettel mit den Daten einer offenbar unbeteiligten Frau. Die Frau sei kontaktiert worden und habe berichtet, dass es bereits ähnliche Fälle in Euskirchen und Bonn gegeben habe, teilte die Polizei mit. Auch dort seien Zettel mit ihrem Namen hinterlassen worden. Ob tatsächlich ein Zusammenhang besteht, war zunächst offen. Mehr zum Thema 1 Min 1 Min Die Polizei bittet um Hinweise aus der Bevölkerung. Angaben zur Schadenshöhe lagen zunächst nicht vor.

articles.title: AfD-Brandmauer: Hessens Regierungschef Boris Rhein plädiert für Ausschussposten für AfD
articles.excerpt: Der hessische Ministerpräsident Boris Rhein (CDU) plädiert im Interview mit dem Magazin "Stern" dafür, der AfD im Bundestag ihr zustehende Vorsitzendenposten in den Fachausschüssen nicht weiter zu verwehren. »Mir ist wichtig: Wir grenzen uns klar von der AfD ab, aber wir grenzen die Partei nicht aus. Das muss auch in der Parlamentsarbeit gelten.« Er sei Anhänger einer Politik der klaren roten Linien, inhaltlich und personell. »Gleichzeitig sollte zum Beispiel die AfD im Bundestag – so wie im Landtag von Hessen und anderen Ländern üblich – Ausschussvorsitze übernehmen können. Die Partei ist gewählt, und so sollte man mit ihr auch umgehen«, sagte Rhein.Er sprach sich auch gegen ein Verbotsverfahren aus. »Nach meiner Wahrnehmung gibt es in unserer Partei eine einhellige Meinung: Wir streben kein AfD-Verbot an.« Das Verfahren würde mindestens fünf Jahre dauern, zudem sei der Ausgang mehr als ungewiss: »Ich rate dazu, die AfD nicht juristisch zu bekämpfen, sondern politisch.« Stimmen verweigertDie AfD hat wie andere Parteien ein Vorschlagsrecht für Ausschussvorsitzende im Bundestag. Bei den Wahlen fielen jedoch alle AfD-Kandidaten durch, weil sie von den Mitgliedern der Gremien nicht gewählt wurden. Der Ausschuss wird dann kommissarisch von einem anderen Abgeordneten geleitet.AfD-Parlamentsgeschäftsführer Bernd Baumann wertete die Überlegungen Rheins als Anzeichen für ein Umdenken in der CDU. Dass der CDU-Politiker sich nun dafür ausspreche, der AfD-Fraktion die ihr zustehenden Ausschussvorsitze im Bundestag zuzugestehen, sei »nur der erste Schritt – weitere werden folgen«, sagte Baumann der Nachrichtenagentur AFP. In den Fachausschüssen des Bundestags findet wichtige gesetzgeberische Arbeit statt. Die Vorsitzendenposten in diesen Gremien werden unter den Fraktionen nach einem bestimmten Schlüssel aufgeteilt. Die jeweilige Fraktion hat dann das Vorschlagsrecht. Die vorgeschlagenen Kandidaten müssen aber von den Ausschussmitgliedern gewählt werden.
